# Ranjith

## Study background
M.Sc. Electrical Systems Engineering (Signal & Information Processing) at Universität Paderborn.

## Interests
- Python backends and automation (Django, FastAPI, data pipelines)
- Computer vision on real hardware – e.g. sorting recyclables on a conveyor belt
- Reinforcement learning for drone navigation, with LLM-written reward functions

## Fun fact
I'm building a kitchen staff-tracking system that uses LiDAR instead of cameras – so nobody gets filmed.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today
AI is great at boilerplate, glue code and getting unstuck, and it has made me noticeably faster. But it's confidently wrong often enough that you still need to understand every line it writes. The bottleneck has shifted from typing code to reviewing it, and most teams haven't adjusted for that yet.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years
Engineers will spend more time specifying, reviewing and testing than writing code by hand, with agents handling much of the implementation. The valuable skills will be system design, knowing the domain, and judging whether the output is actually correct. Codebases will grow faster than anyone can read them, so testing and observability will matter more than ever.

## My hot take on AI
AI won't replace engineers, but it will expose the ones who never understood the code they were copying.

# Sarpesh

## Study background

## Interests
- Embedded systems and power electronics
- Automation and control systems
- Exploring how AI tools can speed up engineering work

## Fun fact
I spend more time debugging wiring than code, and the wiring usually wins.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today
AI coding agents are great for boilerplate, quick scripts and explaining unfamiliar code. But they still make confident mistakes, so every change needs to be reviewed and tested. Right now they are a strong assistant, not a replacement for understanding the system.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years
Engineers will spend less time typing code and more time specifying, reviewing and verifying what agents produce. Domain knowledge, for example in electrical and embedded systems, will matter even more, because someone has to judge whether the generated solution is actually correct and safe.

## My hot take on AI
An AI that writes code you can't verify isn't saving time; it's just moving the bug to production faster.

# Soumya Bani

## Study background
M.Sc. Computer Science student at Paderborn University, Germany.

## Interests
DevOps, AI and Cloud Computing. I enjoy exploring how existing DevOps tools and workflows can be enhanced with AI integration and automation to solve real-world engineering problems.

## Fun fact
I'm building a multi-agent system for incident management and automation, exploring how AI agents can collaborate to investigate incidents and streamline operational workflows.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today
AI is changing how we write and maintain software, and it's already making developers more productive. However, generating code is only one part of software engineering. Understanding the system, making architectural decisions, debugging, and ensuring reliability and security still require strong engineering fundamentals. I see AI as a powerful engineering assistant, not a replacement for engineering knowledge.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years
I think software engineering will move towards more autonomous, AI-driven workflows, where developers orchestrate agents that can build, test, deploy and monitor applications. The role of engineers will increasingly shift from writing every line of code to designing systems, defining constraints and validating outcomes. Cloud, DevOps and AI will become even more interconnected.

## My hot take on AI
The future belongs to engineers who know what to automate and, more importantly, what not to.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today
Software engineering has already changed a lot: most code is now written by agents, and humans act largely as validators. Still, coding agents struggle to understand requirements and to produce well-structured code (for example, following OOP principles), so human supervision remains necessary.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years
Software engineering will change rapidly. Coding agents are getting better at generating complex code and understanding user requirements from only a few prompts. # Ranjith

## Study background
M.Sc. Electrical Systems Engineering (Signal & Information Processing) at Universität Paderborn.

## Interests
- Python backends and automation (Django, FastAPI, data pipelines)
- Computer vision on real hardware – e.g. sorting recyclables on a conveyor belt
- Reinforcement learning for drone navigation, with LLM-written reward functions

## Fun fact
I'm building a kitchen staff-tracking system that uses LiDAR instead of cameras – so nobody gets filmed.

## What I think about AI in software engineering today
AI is great at boilerplate, glue code and getting unstuck, and it has made me noticeably faster. But it's confidently wrong often enough that you still need to understand every line it writes. The bottleneck has shifted from typing code to reviewing it, and most teams haven't adjusted for that yet.

## Where software engineering will be in 5–10 years
Engineers will spend more time specifying, reviewing and testing than writing code by hand, with agents handling much of the implementation. The valuable skills will be system design, knowing the domain, and judging whether the output is actually correct. Codebases will grow faster than anyone can read them, so testing and observability will matter more than ever.

## My hot take on AI
AI won't replace engineers, but it will expose the ones who never understood the code they were copying.

Status: ACTIVE | Category: Theming

- The toggle MUST be a `<button>` element with the id `theme-toggle`.

- Don't use a checkbox for the toggle.

[SG-18] Dark mode philosophy
Status: ACTIVE | Category: Theming

Users choose their theme, but we start with a sensible default.

- If the user has never chosen a theme, the page SHOULD follow the operating system preference (`prefers-color-scheme`).
- As soon as the user clicks the toggle, their choice wins and is remembered, see the theme persistence document.
- Switching the theme MUST NOT reload the page.

[SG-20] Theme switching mechanics
Status: ACTIVE | Category: Theming

The theme is controlled by one attribute on the root element.

- The `<html>` element MUST carry the attribute `data-theme` with the value `light` or `dark`.
- JavaScript switches the theme by changing this attribute, not by toggling classes on the body.
- The CSS MUST define the colors for each theme with attribute selectors, for example
  `[data-theme="light"] { ... }` and `[data-theme="dark"] { ... }`.
- Components use CSS custom properties (for example `var(--bg)`), so they don't need theme-specific rules.

- The stored value is either `light` or `dark`.
- On page load, read the stored value. If there is none, follow the operating system preference.
- Apply the theme as early as possible to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.

and use the variables everywhere instead of repeating the hex values.

[SG-18] Dark mode philosophy
Status: ACTIVE | Category: Theming

Users choose their theme, but we start with a sensible default.

[SG-20] Theme switching mechanics
Status: ACTIVE | Category: Theming

The theme is controlled by one attribute on the root element.

- The `<html>` element MUST carry the attribute `data-theme` with the value `light` or `dark`.
- JavaScript switches the theme by changing this attribute, not by toggling classes on the body.
- The CSS MUST define the colors for each theme with attribute selectors, for example
  `[data-theme="light"] { ... }` and `[data-theme="dark"] { ... }`.
- Components use CSS custom properties (for example `var(--bg)`), so they don't need theme-specific rules.
